chapter.title: Reading a shop in five numbers

cards.body: In the bazaar, the price tag on one slice tells you almost nothing about the shop behind it. A ₹50 slice can belong to a giant shop cut into billions of slices, and a ₹5,000 slice to a small shop cut into very few. To size up a shop you read five numbers off its board: how big it is, how many years of profit you pay for, where its price has been over the year, and how much cash it hands back.

cards.title: Price is the least useful number
cards.body:
Price is what one share last changed hands for. It moves every second, as you saw in chapter 1. On its own it does not tell you if the company is big or small, or if it is cheap or dear.

Market cap is the price of one share multiplied by the total number of shares. It is the price of the whole shop if you bought every slice. A company with 100 crore shares at ₹200 each has a market cap of ₹20,000 crore. In India, SEBI ranks the 100 biggest companies by market cap as large cap, the next 150 as mid cap, and the rest as small cap.

P/E stands for price to earnings. You take the share price and divide it by the profit the company made per share in one year. The answer is how many years of today's profit you are paying for. A P/E of 20 means you pay 20 years of current profit to own a slice.

A high P/E means buyers expect profit to grow fast, so they pay more now. A low P/E means buyers expect slow growth, or they do not trust the profit. Neither is good or bad by itself, but it is the first number to compare a shop against its rivals.

cards.prompt: Share A trades at ₹50. Share B trades at ₹5,000. Which company is bigger?

options.text: Company A, because a lower price means more people can afford it, so it must be bigger
Company B, because a higher price means a bigger shop
You cannot tell from price alone. You need the number of shares too

whyNot.a: That's affordability of one slice, not size of the shop: how many people can buy a share says nothing about how many shares exist.
whyNot.b: That's the price of one slice, not the whole shop: a ₹5,000 share from a company with very few shares can be a small company.

cards.reteach: Think of a cake. One cake cut into 1,000 slices gives tiny cheap slices. The same cake cut into 10 slices gives big dear slices. The cake is the same size. Share price is the slice price. Market cap is the whole cake.

cards.title: One quote page, five numbers
cards.body:
Say a quote page shows a company at ₹400 a share, with 50 crore shares in total. Multiply them and the market cap is ₹20,000 crore, so this is a mid-sized shop by SEBI's ranking, not a giant.

The page says profit per share last year was ₹20. Divide ₹400 by ₹20 and the P/E is 20. You pay 20 years of today's profit for a slice.

The 52-week high is ₹480 and the low is ₹300. Today's ₹400 sits in the middle of where it has been over the past year.

The company paid ₹8 per share as dividend last year. Divide ₹8 by ₹400 and the dividend yield is 2%. For every ₹100 you put in, you got ₹2 back in cash last year.

cards.title: The other three, and one warning
cards.body:
The 52-week high and low are the highest and lowest prices in the past year. They tell you where today's price sits in its own recent range. Near the high means buyers have been winning lately. Near the low means sellers have. They say nothing about whether the shop is good value.

Dividend yield is the cash the company paid out per share in a year, divided by the price, as a percent. A yield of 2% means ₹2 back for every ₹100 of shares you hold. Many fast-growing companies pay little or nothing, because they keep the profit to grow the shop.

P/E only makes sense when you compare like with like. A bank and a software company earn money in very different ways, so their normal P/E ranges differ. Compare an IT company's P/E with other IT companies, not with a bank.

If a company made a loss, there is no profit to divide by. The quote page then shows P/E as a dash or leaves it blank. That blank is a warning, not a bargain.

cards.prompt: Two IT companies both made a profit last year. Company X has a share price of ₹1,500 and a P/E of 35. Company Y has a share price of ₹4,000 and a P/E of 22. Which is priced lower against its profit?

options.text: Company X, because ₹1,500 is less than ₹4,000
Company Y, because you pay 22 years of profit instead of 35
Company X, because a higher P/E means more profit

whyNot.a: That's the slice price, not the price against profit: the share price alone cannot say which is cheaper.
whyNot.c: That's backwards. P/E is price divided by profit, so a higher P/E means you pay more for each rupee of profit, not that there is more profit.

cards.reteach: P/E is a price tag per rupee of yearly profit. Company X charges ₹35 for every ₹1 of profit it makes. Company Y charges ₹22. Both are IT companies, so the comparison is fair, and Y is the cheaper one against its profit.

cards.body: The common mistake is calling a ₹30 share cheap and a ₹3,000 share expensive. That is judging the shop by the price of one slice. You can spot it in yourself when you feel drawn to a share because the number looks small. Before you call anything cheap or dear, you should be able to say its market cap and its P/E against two rivals in the same sector.

cards.prompt: A quote page shows a P/E of 25. What does that mean?

options.text: The price is 25% above its 52-week low
You are paying 25 years of the company's current yearly profit for each share
The company pays back 25% of your money as dividend each year

whyNot.a: That's the 52-week range, not P/E: the high and low describe where the price has been, not how it compares to profit.
whyNot.c: That's dividend yield, not P/E: yield is cash paid out divided by price, and 25% would be extraordinarily high.

cards.reteach: P/E is price divided by profit per share. If a share costs ₹500 and the company earns ₹20 per share a year, 500 divided by 20 is 25. At today's profit it would take 25 years of earnings to add up to the price you paid.

cards.body: Open your broker app or nseindia.com. Search any Nifty 50 company. Find its market cap and P/E. Write one line: large, mid or small, and how many years of profit the price equals.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now look at a quote page and say whether a company is large or small from its market cap, and whether it is priced high or low against its profit from its P/E.
